The Persistence of Small Things

I want to write about the weight of a ceramic coffee mug in your hand at 6:47 on a Tuesday morning, about how the steam rises in a particular slant when the kitchen window is cracked open to autumn, about the way your thumb finds the chip in the rim without your eyes needing to verify its location. These are the territories I find myself returning to, not because the world lacks grandeur—it contains glaciers and nebulae and the final speeches of dying empires—but because I have come to believe that consciousness itself, that strange accident of matter arranged just so, achieves its most honest expression in the unremarkable moments we almost forget to notice.

Consider the last time you waited for water to boil. Not the abstract concept, but the actual experience: the kettle's initial hum, almost subsonic, before the visible agitation begins. The way sound travels differently through water as it approaches its phase transition. Your own breathing, perhaps slower than you expected, perhaps synchronized with some invisible rhythm you didn't choose. What were you thinking? Probably nothing worth recording in a diary, probably something that evaporated the moment the whistle screamed or the switch clicked. Yet this is where we live, statistically speaking. The average human life contains roughly 28,000 days, and on the vast majority of them, no one falls in love for the first time, no one wins anything, no one receives a diagnosis that rewrites their future. We boil water. We stand in lines. We re-read the same email three times without absorbing it.

There's a particular quality of light that occurs in my apartment around 4:15 in November, when the sun has already begun its descent but hasn't yet committed to sunset. It enters through the west-facing windows at such an angle that it illuminates only the top third of the room, leaving the lower spaces in a kind of premature dusk. Dust motes become visible in this light, performing their Brownian dance with what appears, at that scale, to be something like intention. I've spent perhaps forty hours total of my life watching this light, usually while doing something else—folding laundry, arguing on the phone, staring at a cursor blinking against white. I couldn't tell you what years these hours belonged to, what was happening in the world or in my life during their accumulation. They resist narrative. They refuse to be recruited into any story I might tell about myself.

And yet. I suspect these hours have shaped me more than the documented milestones, the graduations and funerals and departures. They have taught me something about duration, about the texture of time when it isn't being measured against achievement. The philosopher Henri Bergson distinguished between *temps*—mechanical, spatialized time, the time of clocks and calendars—and *durée*, the felt experience of temporal passage, which he argued could only be grasped through intuition rather than analysis. Our November light belongs to *durée*. It cannot be saved or shared; a photograph would capture only its physical correlates, not the quality of attention it elicited, the particular way it made the room feel like a diorama of itself, the strange peace of being simultaneously inside and outside of ordinary life.

I think often about the Japanese concept of *mono no aware*, often translated as "the pathos of things" or "the bittersweet awareness of impermanence." It's most commonly associated with cherry blossoms, with the deliberate cultivation of sorrow at their falling. But I wonder if the concept isn't more radically applicable to the unbeautiful, the unphotographed, the things that leave no trace even in memory. The awareness that this particular configuration of light and dust and half-attention will never recur exactly, even though nothing about it warrants preservation—this seems to me a more profound and more difficult pathos. The cherry blossom has cultural scaffolding to support its significance. The Tuesday morning mug does not. We must build our own scaffolding, or else recognize that some experiences are meant to stand without it, architecture-free, momentary shelters that we inhabit and abandon without record.

There's a practice I've developed, half-consciously, over years of urban living: the identification of neighborhood trees. Not the official names—I rarely know whether I'm looking at a London plane or a silver maple—but the informal christenings that come from repeated encounter. The tree that grows at a forty-degree angle from the sidewalk crack on 47th Street, its trunk wrapped in the remnants of a "Missing Cat" poster from 2019. The ginkgo on the corner that drops its fruit in October, releasing a smell that my brain has learned to associate with the beginning of academic years, with new notebooks and the anxiety of unmet potential. These trees are not beautiful in any conventional sense. They are urban survivors, compromised by pollution and compacted soil, often butchered by municipal pruning. But they are mine in a way that curated park landscapes cannot be. I have watched them through illness and health, through relationships that formed and dissolved, through political catastrophes that seemed to alter the atmospheric pressure of ordinary days. They have been present without demanding presence, the best kind of companions.

The anthropologist Tim Ingold writes about "the meshwork" of lived experience, a tangle of lines rather than a network of nodes. We do not, he suggests, move from point to point through life; rather, we wayfare, our paths weaving in and out of others' paths, with no clear origin or destination. The tree on 47th Street is a point in my meshwork, but more importantly, it's part of the line, the ongoing process of being-in-the-world that resists extraction and summary. I cannot tell you what the tree means. I can only tell you that I have passed it approximately 1,200 times, that I have noticed it perhaps 400 of those times, that I have thought about it deliberately maybe 50 times, and that these frequencies constitute a relationship that no single encounter could adequately represent.

This is the difficulty with writing about the small and persistent: it scales poorly. The essay demands a shape, an arc, a justification for the reader's attention. But my subject resists such demands. It sprawls, it repeats, it accumulates without climax. Like the dust that settles on the books I mean to read, like the slight stiffness in my left shoulder that has become baseline rather than complaint, like the particular silence of my apartment at 2 AM when the refrigerator compressor cycles off and I can hear, or imagine I hear, the building's structural settling, its decades of accumulated weight adjusting in microscopic increments.

I want to make a case for the value of this resistance, though I recognize the irony of making a case at all. Perhaps I can only gesture toward it, offer examples that might resonate or might not, depending on the meshwork of your own life. The smell of rain on hot asphalt—petrichor, the geologists call it, from the Greek for "stone" and "the fluid that flows in the veins of the gods." The particular fatigue of your eyes after hours of reading physical pages versus illuminated screens. The way a familiar voice sounds different through a telephone speaker, stripped of its upper harmonics, made strange by technological mediation. These are not experiences we seek out. They happen to us, or more precisely, they happen around us, and we happen to be present, which is itself a kind of happening, though one we rarely credit.

The pandemic years revealed something about this presence, or its absence. For those who experienced lockdown, there was a strange magnification of the small: the daily walk, the same loop through the same streets, became charged with significance it had previously lacked. People reported noticing birdsong for the first time, not because the birds had changed, but because the traffic had diminished, because their own attention had shifted from the productive to the perceptual. Then, gradually or suddenly, the old rhythms returned, and many of these noticings were subsumed again, lost not through forgetting but through a kind of active demotion, a recognition that sustained attention to the unremarkable is incompatible with the demands of ordinary life.

I don't want to romanticize this. There is a reason we demote. The unremarkable, attended to too exclusively, becomes the terrain of mental illness, of obsessive compulsion, of the inability to prioritize that we call, in clinical contexts, dysfunction. The person who cannot stop noticing the pattern of floor tiles, who is trapped in the texture of each moment without the ability to synthesize or move forward, is not experiencing a heightened form of life but a disrupted one. The small things must be allowed to remain small; they must not be made to carry more weight than they can bear. This is the delicate balance: to notice without grasping, to value without instrumentalizing, to let the Tuesday morning mug be simply what it is, neither a symbol of domestic contentment nor an emblem of spiritual emptiness, but a ceramic vessel containing a heated liquid, warming your hands, soon to be empty, soon to be washed or left unwashed, soon to be forgotten until next Tuesday or the Tuesday after.

I think of the poet Francis Ponge, who wrote extended prose poems about ordinary objects: the orange, the candle, the piece of bread. His method was to approach these things with a kind of radical equality, refusing the hierarchy that would place them below grander subjects. But even Ponge was making art, was shaping his attention into forms that could be received, that asked for the reader's time as something owed. The true persistence of small things, the thing I'm trying to write toward, exists prior to and outside of such making. It is the unwritten, the unwritable, the experiences that dissolve even as we attempt to hold them in language's solution.

Perhaps this is why I return to the mug, to the light, to the tree. Not to capture them, which is impossible, but to acknowledge them, to perform a kind of witness that expects no outcome. The world is full of such witnessing, most of it invisible, most of it performed without the witness knowing they are performing. The elderly person who watches the same pigeons every day from the same park bench. The night shift worker who learns the particular sounds of a building's empty hours. The child who stares at the ceiling during a fever, watching patterns form and dissolve in the textured plaster. These are not preparations for anything. They are not practice. They are simply what consciousness does when it is not recruited for purpose, and they constitute, I am increasingly convinced, the majority of what we call a life.

The challenge, then, is to find a way of valuing this majority without betraying it through valuation itself. To say that the small things matter is already to make them matter, to drag them into the economy of significance where they may not wish to participate. Better, perhaps, to say that they persist, and that we persist alongside them, in a kind of parallel existence that occasionally becomes aware of itself, as I am aware now, writing this, of the particular sound of my own breathing, the slight ache in my lower back from sitting too long, the quality of light in this room that will have changed by the time you read these words, that has already changed, that is changing now, in the time it takes to complete this sentence, this paragraph, this act of attention that wanted only to say: I was here. I noticed. It was enough.
